chapter.title: Natural or Cultured Pearls, Precious or Semiprecious Stones, Precious Metals, Metals Clad With Precious Metal, and Articles Thereof; Imitation Jewelry; Coin

page.h1: HTS Chapter 71: Natural or Cultured Pearls, Precious or Semiprecious Stones, Precious Metals, Metals Clad With Precious Metal, and Articles Thereof; Imitation Jewelry; Coin — U.S. Export Rules & Ways to Pay Less Abroad

seo.title: Chapter 71 Export Rules: Kimberley Process, AML & Schedule B
seo.shortDescription: What a U.S. gold, diamond or jewelry exporter must do before shipping: Schedule B, Kimberley Process certificate, anti-money-laundering rules and Russia luxury-goods limits.

intro: Most of this chapter's trade, bullion, needs no Commerce licence: find the Schedule B number, screen the buyer, check sanctions and file the export in AES. The chapter-specific rules are compliance rules. Rough diamonds need a Kimberley Process certificate, dealers in precious metals, stones and jewels must run an anti-money-laundering program, and exports of listed luxury goods, which include jewelry and precious stones, to Russia and Belarus are barred.

steps.title: Find the Schedule B number
steps.whatToDo: Look up the 10-digit Schedule B number for each product with the Census Bureau's free search tool. Its first six digits are the same as the HS code every country uses, so it also tells you which line of the buyer's tariff applies. The U.S. import (HTS) number and the Schedule B number match only to six digits.
steps.when: Every export. It goes on the export filing (the last step) and on the commercial invoice.
steps.chapterNote: Most of the chapter is gold, Schedule B 7108.12 (non-monetary gold in other unwrought forms), then other precious-metal articles (7115.90), jewelry (7113.19), 7108.13 (semi-manufactured gold), rough and polished diamonds (7102) and silver (7106.91). The first six digits are the HS code on the Overview.

steps.title: Screen the buyer and everyone in the deal
steps.whatToDo: Check the buyer, the end user and any agent against the Consolidated Screening List. It combines the Commerce lists (Entity List, Denied Persons, Unverified, Military End-User), the State Department lists and the Treasury (OFAC) sanctions lists of parties you may not deal with, or may deal with only under a licence.
steps.when: Every export, before you accept the order.
steps.chapterNote: Bullion is sold through banks, refiners and vault operators. Screen the named buyer and, where you can, the ultimate consignee, especially for shipments through trading hubs.

steps.title: Check whether you need an export licence
steps.whatToDo: Find the product's Export Control Classification Number (ECCN) on the Commerce Control List. Most goods are not listed and are EAR99. For a listed ECCN, look up the destination on the Commerce Country Chart under each reason for control: an X means a licence is needed unless a licence exception applies. Even EAR99 goods need a licence for embargoed countries and for restricted end users or end uses.
steps.when: Every export of goods subject to the Export Administration Regulations (EAR).
steps.chapterNote: Gold, silver, platinum-group metals, diamonds and jewelry are generally EAR99, so no Commerce licence is needed. Rough diamonds need a Kimberley Process certificate instead, and exports of listed luxury goods to Russia and Belarus need a licence that is not granted in the ordinary case (see Agency rules below).

steps.title: Check sanctions on the destination
steps.whatToDo: Check the destination against OFAC's sanctions programs and the EAR's embargo rules. Cuba, Iran and North Korea have country-wide rules, and Syria still needs a Commerce licence for most items; Russia and Belarus need a licence for any item with an ECCN. Several programs have special permissions for food and medicine.
steps.when: Exports to a sanctioned or embargoed country, or to a listed person anywhere.
steps.chapterNote: OFAC and BIS sanctions close sales to embargoed destinations and listed persons. Russia and Belarus have the extra luxury-goods limits described below.

steps.title: File the export in AES (Electronic Export Information)
steps.whatToDo: You (the U.S. principal party in interest) or your freight forwarder file the EEI in the Automated Export System — free through ACE AESDirect — and put the confirmation number (ITN) on the shipping documents. File at least 24 hours before an ocean shipment is loaded, 2 hours before a flight departs, or 1 hour before a truck reaches the border. Not filing can cost a civil penalty of up to $17,412 per violation.
steps.when: When one Schedule B number in one shipment to one buyer is worth over $2,500, and at any value when the shipment needs a Commerce licence or a DEA permit or declaration, or ships an EAR item to Cuba, Iran, North Korea or Syria, or a Commerce Control List item to China, Russia or Venezuela.
steps.chapterNote: Bullion shipments are almost always over $2,500 per Schedule B number, so file in AES. Rough diamonds also carry the Kimberley Process certificate number in the AES record.

rules.agency: U.S. Kimberley Process Authority (State, Treasury OFAC and Census)
rules.title: Rough diamonds (HTS 7102.10, 7102.21, 7102.31): every export needs a Kimberley Process certificate issued by the U.S. Kimberley Process Authority or a licensed entity, whatever the value. File the shipment in AES, put the AES filing number on the certificate and give the certificate to the Census Bureau immediately after export. Keep a copy for five years.

citations.label: Federal Register: Rough Diamonds Control Regulations (31 CFR Part 592)
Federal Register: Requirement for reporting the Kimberley Process certificate number for exports

rules.title: Anti-money-laundering program: a dealer in precious metals, precious stones or jewels, meaning one that bought and sold more than $50,000 of covered goods in the prior year, must have an anti-money-laundering program that includes customer due diligence and compliance training.

citations.label: 31 CFR Part 1027 (anti-money-laundering programs for dealers in precious metals, stones or jewels)

rules.agency: Commerce Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS)
rules.title: Russia and Belarus luxury goods: BIS requires a licence, which is not granted in the ordinary case, to export listed luxury goods to Russia and Belarus. The list in Supplement No. 5 to Part 746 includes jewelry and precious stones; check the supplement for the exact HTS codes and value limits.

citations.label: BIS: Supplement No. 5 to Part 746 (luxury goods)
BIS: EAR Part 746 (embargoes and other special controls)

groups.label: Pearls, natural or cultured (loose or temporarily strung)
groups.note: Pearls: routine, apart from the Russia and Belarus luxury-goods limits.

groups.label: Diamonds, unmounted — rough, polished and industrial
groups.note: Diamonds: rough diamonds (7102.10, 7102.21, 7102.31) need a Kimberley Process certificate; polished diamonds do not, but the Russia and Belarus limits and dealer AML rules apply.

groups.label: Rubies, sapphires, emeralds & other gemstones (unmounted)
groups.note: Precious and semi-precious stones: routine apart from the Russia and Belarus limits and dealer AML rules.

groups.label: Silver — bullion, doré, bars, powder
groups.note: Silver bullion: no Commerce licence; dealer AML rules apply.

groups.label: Base metals clad with silver
groups.note: Base metals clad with silver: routine.

groups.label: Gold — bullion, doré, bars, powder, leaf, monetary gold
groups.note: Gold: no Commerce licence for bullion; dealer AML rules apply and sanctions limit restricted destinations.

groups.label: Base metals or silver clad with gold
groups.note: Base metals or silver clad with gold: routine.

groups.label: Platinum, palladium, rhodium, iridium, osmium & ruthenium
groups.note: Platinum-group metals: no Commerce licence; dealer AML rules apply.

groups.label: Precious-metal waste, scrap & ash
groups.note: Precious-metal scrap and ash: routine, apart from sanctions on restricted destinations.

groups.label: Jewelry of gold, silver, platinum or clad metal
groups.note: Jewelry: routine apart from the Russia and Belarus luxury-goods limits and dealer AML rules.

groups.label: Silverware & goldsmiths' wares (tableware, flatware)
groups.note: Silverware and goldsmiths' wares: routine, apart from the Russia and Belarus limits.

groups.label: Other precious-metal articles — minted bars, platinum gauze
groups.note: Other precious-metal articles: dealer AML rules apply where the goods are precious metals.

groups.label: Articles of pearls & gemstones (strands, gemstone jewelry, carvings)
groups.note: Articles of pearls and stones: routine, apart from the Russia and Belarus limits.

groups.label: Coins — bullion coins and other coin

savings.title: Claim the free-trade-agreement rate abroad
savings.saves: The partner country's tariff on qualifying U.S. goods — often 0% instead of its normal rate.
savings.appliesTo: Goods that meet the agreement's rules of origin, shipped to one of the 20 U.S. free-trade-agreement partners: Australia, Bahrain, Canada, Chile, Colombia, Costa Rica, Dominican Republic, El Salvador, Guatemala, Honduras, Israel, Jordan, Korea, Mexico, Morocco, Nicaragua, Oman, Panama, Peru and Singapore.
savings.document: A certification of origin from the exporter, producer or importer, which the buyer uses to claim the rate at import. For USMCA there is no set form, but it must contain the nine data elements in Annex 5-A.
savings.caveat: Whoever certifies must be able to back it up: for USMCA, a U.S. exporter or producer keeps origin records for at least 5 years, gives CBP a copy on request and tells buyers promptly about errors. Check the product's rule of origin and the partner's rate in the FTA Tariff Tool first.

savings.title: Get U.S. duty back on imported inputs (drawback)
savings.saves: 99% of the U.S. import duties, taxes and fees paid on goods or materials that are exported, or used to make the goods you export.
savings.appliesTo: Imported goods exported unused, and imported materials used to make an exported product (or, under the substitution rules, goods of the same kind).
savings.document: An electronic drawback claim in ACE, filed within 5 years of the import date, with the import and export records that tie the two together.
savings.caveat: Antidumping and countervailing duties are not refunded, and CBP takes no paper claims. The refund is on U.S. duties only; it does not lower the buyer's tariff.

disclaimer: This page summarizes U.S. export rules to help you find the right regulation; it is not legal advice. Rules change and depend on the exact product, buyer and destination — check the cited regulation and the agency before you ship.
